syllabusTopics: Dalton's atomic theory and its postulates
Avogadro's law and some deductions: molecular mass and vapour density, molecular mass and volume of gas, molecular mass and number of particles
Mole and its relation with mass, volume and number of particles
Theoretical yield, experimental yield and % yield
Calculation of empirical and molecular formula from % composition (solving related numerical problems)

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The **laws of stoichiometry** — conservation of mass (Lavoisier), definite proportions (Proust), multiple proportions (Dalton), reciprocal proportions (Richter) and Gay-Lussac's gaseous volumes — fix how much of each element reacts. Definite proportions fixes one compound's composition; multiple proportions compares ratios across compounds of the same element pair (CO 1:2 vs CO₂ with oxygen per 12 g C).…

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Definite vs multiple proportions:** definite = one compound, one fixed ratio; multiple = several compounds of the same two elements, ratio of ratios.  ·  **Gay-Lussac's law vs Avogadro's law:** Gay-Lussac compares reacting *volumes*; Avogadro explains it — equal volumes contain equal *molecules*.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "A pure compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed proportion by mass" — Proust.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***NO, NO₂, N₂O*** — oxygen per 14 g nitrogen: 8, 16, 32 g → ratio 1:2:4, a perfect multiple-proportions triplet.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Rules the Mole Obey Before any calculation, chemistry agrees on five quantitative laws: mass is conserved, composition is definite, ratios are multiple, equivalents are reciprocal, and reacting gas volumes are simple. Together with Avogadro's law they are the **laws of stoichiometry** — the grammar of every balanced equation.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The five laws at a glance | Law | Scientist | Statement | |---|---|---| | **Conservation of mass** | Lavoisier (1789) | Total mass of reactants = total mass of products in a chemical reaction | | **Definite proportions** | Proust (1799) | A pure compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed proportion by mass | | **Multiple proportions** | Dalton (1803) |…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "CDMR-G: Conservation, Definite, Multiple, Reciprocal, Gay-Lussac — five laws, five scientists."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): State the law of multiple proportions and illustrate it with carbon oxides.** — Statement: when two elements form more than one compound, masses of one combining with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio. In CO, C:O = 12:16; in CO₂, C:O = 12:32.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Always attach the scientist's name to the law — NEB awards the name as a separate mark.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Fixed-mass reference** — in multiple and reciprocal proportions, always divide by the mass of the fixed element before comparing.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Five laws: conservation of mass (Lavoisier), definite proportions (Proust), multiple proportions (Dalton), reciprocal proportions (Richter), gaseous volumes (Gay-Lussac). Each needs a one-line statement plus one numeric illustration.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: These laws are empirical: they were measured before atoms were believed in — and their existence is itself evidence for atoms.
